name: Grey Green
lede: Grey green is a descriptive name for a muted green, best known in the books through celadon, the pale Chinese glaze, and through the way distance dulls foliage.

sections.title: A name made of two words
sections.body:
Grey Green is a plain description rather than a historical name: a muted, slightly yellowish green [7]. Our library files the swatch under ISCC-NBS 1955 as "moderate yellowish green" (block 150), and the xkcd color survey lists a near twin at #86A17D [7]. Its nearest everyday names are [[moss]], at a color difference of 8.3, and [[greyish-green]], a sibling less than two units away [7].

Books mostly use the words for things, not as a color with a history. The rest of this page follows where they appear.

sections.title: Celadon, the grey-green with a history
sections.body:
The best-known grey green in the books is celadon. Finlay says the word is the generic name given to all Chinese gray-green porcelain [1]. St Clair traces the European word to Céladon, a shepherd dressed in pale green in a French novel of 1607; Finlay also offers a theory involving Saladin and hedges it [2][1].

A popular belief says celadon ware detects poison. It is a legend: Finlay reports that the Mughal emperor Jahangir's test showed it did not [1]. The color is [[celadon]] in our data, and the word covers a range, not one swatch.

sections.title: Words for a grey green
sections.body: Latin had no common word for this color and leaned on one. Pastoureau lists *glaucus* as gray-green, greenish or bluish green, while *viridis* occupies nearly the whole range of green [3]. English kept the first as [[glaucous]], which St Clair's glossary defines as a pale gray blue-green, and gave *French gray* to a very pale gray-green [9].

sections.title: Where to see it
sections.body:
Distance turns green to grey green. Gurney notes that warm foliage fades to a gray-green or blue-green as it recedes, because far colors lose saturation [4]. The same leaves can look sharp yellow-green when light shines through them and gray-green on their upper surface [4]. The practical eye-training habit is to look at a tree line and name the grey in it before you name the green.

Pigments drift this way too. The Pigment Compendium says zinc yellow tends to darken in light into a grey-green, through the formation of chromium oxide [5]. A nature book on pigment sources photographs a grey-green vivianite powder, a reminder that minerals give the color first [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 87 contain this grey green on at least five per cent of the canvas, within six color-distance units [8]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a match is not a pigment test [8].

The earliest is Francesco Botticini's Madonna and Child with Tobias and the Angel Raphael, about 1470 [8]. The 1900s hold 21 of 1,674 paintings, 3.43 times the archive rate, and the 1910s peak at 8 of 523 [8]. Austria stands out, with 8 of 121 paintings, and Impressionism has 6 of 140 [8]. The largest single match is Klimt's [[painting:commons-Q17495516|Rosebushes under the Trees]] of 1905, where it covers 44 per cent of the canvas [8]. Renoir's [[painting:nga-1211|The Dancer]] of 1874 reaches 33 per cent [8].

By lightness, 39 per cent of the matching area sits in highlights, 51 per cent in the midtones and 10 per cent in shadows [8].

openers: Distance is a grey-green mixer: far foliage loses saturation and drifts to gray-green.
Celadon is the generic name for Chinese gray-green porcelain.

issues: Etymology attributed to St Clair only; Finlay gives the Saladin theory
